The Rashidun Caliphate. From 632 to 661 of the common era, this comprises the first four Islamic caliphs—Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, and Ali—who were chosen from Muhammad's companions and governed the early Islamic state as it rapidly conquered the Byzantine and Persian empires. This brief period established the institutional foundation for Islamic governance, Islamic law, and the territorial base of the Islamic world, though it ended in civil conflict that would shape Islamic politics forever.

The Rashidun encompassed the reigns of four caliphs who were elected or appointed rather than dynastic successors. Umar's reign from 634 to 644 saw the most explosive expansion—conquest of Syria, Iraq, Egypt, and parts of Persia—transforming the caliphate into a true empire. The Rashidun established the shura, the consultative assembly principle, and early Islamic administrative structures that later dynasties would modify but not abandon. Under Caliph Uthman they standardized the Qur'an, creating an official written text to prevent variant readings. Yet Uthman's rule sparked the Fitna, a civil war, as rival factions disputed whether leadership should be elective or hereditary. This schism defined the Sunni-Shiite division. The caliphate ended when Ali ibn Abi Talib was assassinated in 661, followed by his rival Mu'awiyah I establishing the Umayyad dynasty.

The Prophet Muhammad came before them—his companions formed the caliphate after his death. The Umayyad Caliphate succeeded them and shifted to hereditary Arab rule. The Abbasid Caliphate later overthrew the Umayyads and claimed to restore consultative governance. And Islamic law itself was codified during the Rashidun era with the development of hadith and foundational jurisprudence.
